newsitem.title: USA: Police arrest suspect in U.S. murder of five women.
newsitem.headline: Police arrest suspect in U.S. murder of five women.

text.p: A man accused of the murder of five women at a house in Oklahoma City in 1992 has been arrested in California after DNA tests linked him to the killings, officials said Wednesday.
FBI agents and San Jose police officers arrested Danny Hooks, 38, Tuesday at a construction site in San Jose where he worked, an FBI spokesman said. He was being held in Santa Clara County Jail.
Hooks was recently charged in Oklahoma City with the murder of five women found stabbed to death in a house there on May 16, 1992, Oklahoma City police spokesman Captain Ted Carlton said.
He said detectives from Oklahoma travelled to San Jose on Wednesday to interview Hooks and that Oklahoma authorities would seek his extradition to face the murder charges.
Carlton said the murders were "very brutal." The five women were found naked and several had been bound or blindfolded, he said. He said police did not know the motive for the murders.
Work by the California Department of Justice's DNA databank in Berkeley, California, helped identify Hooks as a suspect, California officials said.
Hooks was convicted of rape, kidnapping and assault with a deadly weapon in Contra Costa County in northern California in 1988, the California Department of Justice said.

Before his release from state prison in 1991, Hooks was required to leave blood and saliva samples for DNA profiling and entry into the state's convicted felon DNA databank in Berkeley. California law allowed samples to be taken from sexual and violent offenders freed from prison.

A DNA profile derived from bloodstains left at the Oklahoma crime scene was sent to California for comparison against the state's DNA databanks and a "match" was made with Hooks, the California Department of Justice said.
"This is the fourth unsolved murder case the state's DNA databank has cracked and it is one more example of the power of DNA evidence analysis," California Attorney General Dan Lungren said.
Oklahoma City police said they had worked hard to try to solve the murder case since 1992, fingerprinting more than 8,000 people and taking blood samples from 400 people.
Officials said the delay in matching the DNA was partly because the nation's DNA databases were still evolving.

The Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation's DNA lab became operational in 1994. It obtained a profile of the unknown killer's DNA in 1995 and sent the profile to states which had DNA databases in the following year. The California lab came up with the positive match last month.
Oklahoma City police said they had confirmed that Hooks was in Oklahoma City on the date of the murders.
